topic: burning charcoal in an earth covered stack: draught holes, smoke colour and sealing the burn

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr sondowy w kopcu

base: I am burning charcoal in an earth covered stack for the first time this autumn.
A steel retort drum stands at the edge of the clearing and I have used it before.
A probe thermometer goes into the side of the stack and reads the inside temperature.
The earth stack has been smoking heavily for six hours and the smoke is still white.
Should I open more draught holes now, or wait until the smoke changes colour?
Wait for the colour, because white smoke simply means the wood is still giving up water.
Opening holes now pulls air through and burns the very wood you want to keep.
When the smoke thins and turns blue, the water has gone and the charring begins.
Only then should you start closing holes to slow the burn down and hold the heat.
The smoke turned blue after eleven hours and I began closing the lower holes.
One side of the stack now smokes far harder than the other, which worries me.
The probe thermometer reads three hundred on the busy side and half that opposite.
The retort drum never showed such a difference, but it was small and evenly packed.
Should I close the hot side down hard, or open the cold side to even things out?
Open the cold side, because closing the hot side simply pushes the burn sideways.
An uneven stack usually means the earth covering is thinner where the smoke escapes.
Throw a shovel of damp earth onto the busy side and watch the smoke slow.
Even burning matters more than speed, since a fast stack leaves you brands and ash.
Adding earth to the hot side evened the smoke within about half an hour.
The stack burned steadily all night and settled by roughly a foot before morning.
The smoke is now very thin and almost clear against the trees behind the clearing.
Does that mean the burn is finished, or is there still wood charring underneath?
Thin clear smoke means the burn is done and the stack must be sealed immediately.
Close every hole with earth and let the whole thing cool for two full days.
Air reaching hot charcoal will burn your entire week of work into a heap of ash.
Do not be tempted to open it early, however quiet the stack appears from outside.
I sealed the stack and left it for three days before opening the top.
The charcoal is good and black, though the outer layer is soft and crumbles easily.
The middle rings when I drop a piece, which I take to be a good sign.
Is the crumbly outer layer worth keeping, or should I return it to the next stack?
Return it, because soft charcoal has charred too fast and burns away without much heat.
It sits at the edge where the earth covering was thinnest and the air reached it.
Next time build the covering thicker at the outside than you think strictly necessary.
Broken pieces go back into the middle of the following stack and char properly there.
The second stack had a much thicker covering and produced far less crumbly charcoal.
The whole burn took two days rather than one, which surprised me a little.
The yield looks better by weight, though I have not measured it carefully yet.
Is a slower burn always better, or is there a point where patience stops paying?
There is such a point, and you are close to it with a two day burn.
Below a certain heat the wood chars unevenly and leaves brands through the whole stack.
Aim for a steady burn that finishes in about thirty hours for a stack that size.
Weigh the next yield properly, because guessing at charcoal by eye deceives almost everybody.
